<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p">Equal contribution, ordered by coin flip</p>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="1" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 1 1" width="1"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,1) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><foreignObject overflow="visible"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">GPWM</span></span></foreignObject></g></svg></span>: Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Robert Ren
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span></span>

</span></span>

<span class="ltx_personname">Yikai Tang

<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jianing Zhang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sergey Zakharov
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Pavel Tokmakov
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Katerina Fragkiadaki
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="abstract1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="1" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 1 1" width="1"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,1) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><foreignObject overflow="visible"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">GPWM</span></span></foreignObject></g></svg></span>, a <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">G</span>enerative <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">P</span>article
<span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">W</span>orld <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M</span>odel that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by
generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene
appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single
representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and
granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction.
GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines
flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical
trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate
GPWM on <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse
geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments.
GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average.
Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single <em id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Unified</em> GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains.
GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties,
object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables
contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint
actuator–object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained
actions, planning searches the model’s latent noise for interactions
that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model,
noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on
pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to
discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve
goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or
goal-specific policies.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/GPWM_teaser_v25.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/254;" width="476" height="254" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GPWM learns 3D particle dynamics across six physical domains.<span id="S0.F1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Top: samples from the six domains of <span id="S0.F1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>. Middle: given the observed frames and a noisy
future, a U-shaped multi-resolution spatio-temporal transformer denoises the future motion of
every particle. Bottom: GPWM (the better of its specialist and unified models in each domain)
lowers prediction error relative to the strongest baseline in every domain, by 31% on average, rolls out
55<math id="S0.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> past its 16-frame training window, simulates 3D dynamics from images, and plans via
guided diffusion, succeeding at picking where action-space search fails.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A general-purpose physical world model should predict how a 3D scene
evolves and how to act to bring it toward a desired state. This requires
modeling diverse objects and materials, maintaining coherent dynamics
over long horizons, and reasoning through physical contact.
Recent generative video world models capture rich and multimodal scene
evolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bruce et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2026</a>)</cite>,
but generate visual appearance rather than explicitly representing the
motion and interactions of physical objects in 3D.
Particle- and point-based models instead represent physical state
directly in 3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pfaff et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duisterhof et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. However, existing learned 3D
dynamics models are typically limited by deterministic prediction,
short generation horizons, or specialization to particular materials
and interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
We ask: <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">can a generative model of 3D particle motion capture
diverse physical dynamics, predict over long horizons, and support
planning through contact?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce GPWM, a generative world model that represents 3D
scenes as particles and rigid bodies and predicts their motion over
time (Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Deformable objects are modeled through
particle displacements and rigid bodies through body-level
transformations, providing a common representation for rigid,
deformable, cloth, and granular dynamics.
GPWM conditions on observed 3D scene history and, when available,
physical properties and future actuator motion. Actuators share the
same geometric representation as other scene components, allowing
their trajectories to either condition physical prediction or be
generated jointly with object motion for planning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Learning generative particle dynamics at scale presents two challenges:
scenes may contain thousands of particles across interacting objects,
and prediction errors accumulate over long rollouts.
GPWM addresses the first with object-aware multi-resolution
tokenization and spatio-temporal attention in relative 3D coordinates.
To address the second, we combine flow matching with
<em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diffusion forcing</em>, independently varying noise levels across
future frames. This enables <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">streaming generation</em>, where
near-future states are progressively resolved and committed while
farther-future states remain uncertain and revisable, allowing
generation far beyond the training horizon.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We train and evaluate GPWM on <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>, a corpus of 25.5 million
simulated frames spanning rigid, elastic, elastoplastic, granular,
and cloth dynamics, with diverse geometries, physical properties,
interactions, and robot embodiments.
Unlike prior learned dynamics models trained for individual physical
domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, we also train a single
<em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Unified</em> GPWM across heterogeneous physical regimes.
Across six domains, the best GPWM variant reduces prediction
error by 31% on average relative to the strongest applicable prior
baseline. Remarkably, the Unified model outperforms domain-specific
specialists on Dragging and Pick and Place, demonstrating that heterogeneous
physical dynamics can be learned within one set of weights.
GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical
properties, object counts, and long rollout horizons.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond prediction, GPWM learns a <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generative prior over
physical interactions</em> that enables contact-rich planning.
Conventional action-space planning searches actuator commands and
predicts their consequences, but can struggle to discover complex
contact sequences or exploit world-model errors through
out-of-distribution actions. By jointly generating actuator and
object trajectories, GPWM instead allows planning in its latent
noise space, biasing search toward learned interaction patterns.
We optimize this noise using either gradient-based latent noise
optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eyring et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ben-Hamu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karunratanakul et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or gradient-free sampling, guided by
sparse rewards on desired object configurations.
Using the same world model, noise-space planning substantially
outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking.
The resulting actuator trajectories execute successfully in
simulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific
policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are as follows.
<span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> We introduce <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPWM</span>, a generative world model
that predicts the motion of particles and rigid bodies across
heterogeneous physical regimes, with streaming generation far
beyond its training horizon.
<span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> We introduce <span id="S1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>, a 25.5M-frame corpus
spanning diverse physical dynamics, interactions, and robot embodiments.
<span id="S1.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3)</span> GPWM achieves <span id="S1.p6.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">state-of-the-art physical prediction</span>
across diverse domains, generalizes to unseen geometries, physical
properties, object counts, and rollout horizons, and demonstrates
that a single Unified model can outperform domain-specific specialists.
<span id="S1.p6.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(4)</span> We demonstrate <span id="S1.p6.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">contact-rich planning through
generative interaction priors</span>, showing that searching the learned
distribution of actuator–object trajectories is substantially more
effective than direct action-space optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Physics simulators and learned 3D dynamics.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Physics engines and differentiable simulators use explicit physical models for
prediction and control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Todorov et al., 2012</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, while learned
simulators infer dynamics from trajectory data using particle and mesh
representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pfaff et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
RoboCraft <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and RoboCook <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2023</a>)</cite> model
elastoplastic manipulation; ParticleFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> models multi-object,
multi-material interactions; RigidFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dou et al., 2026</a>)</cite> targets
multi-object rigid dynamics; and Particle-Grid Neural Dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> uses a hybrid particle-grid representation for
deformable dynamics. PointWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> represents scene
motion and robot actions as 3D point flows for forecasting and model-predictive
control. These learned 3D dynamics models are predominantly domain-specific
and deterministic. Deterministic prediction becomes increasingly restrictive
as physical diversity grows: contact and interaction uncertainty can induce
multiple plausible futures that must otherwise collapse to a single
trajectory. GPWM instead learns a generative distribution over dynamics
within a common architecture spanning rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular
systems.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generative physical dynamics and long-horizon prediction.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The closest works to GPWM are PhysCtrl <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> and
PhysiFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. PhysCtrl generates 3D point
trajectories conditioned on physical parameters and forces across rigid,
elastic, sand, and plasticine materials. PhysiFormer uses a diffusion
transformer with attention factorized across space, time, and objects to
generate multi-object rigid and elastic trajectories. Both are trained over fixed,
relatively short generation horizons and retain the full set of 3D points or
vertices throughout the network, limiting scalability to densely represented
scenes; PhysiFormer, for example, trains on scenes with at most 356 vertices.
Both are also trained on substantially smaller datasets than <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>.
In contrast, GPWM progressively compresses particles through a
multi-resolution hierarchy, scaling to scenes with up to 12,000 particles,
and combines this spatial scalability with diffusion
forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for stable auto-regressive generation far beyond the
training horizon.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generative models for planning.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffuser <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and Decision Diffuser <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ajay et al., 2022</a>)</cite>
formulate decision making as trajectory generation conditioned or guided
by task objectives. Subsequent work explores adaptive
planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, hierarchical trajectory
generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and joint state–action generation for
control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
Classifier- and reward-guided sampling typically steer intermediate
noisy states during generation, while latent noise optimization (LNO),
including D-Flow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ben-Hamu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Diffusion Noise
Optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karunratanakul et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, optimizes the initial
noise by differentiating through the generative process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPWM extends these ideas to contact-rich planning in 3D physical
environments. By jointly generating actuator and object trajectories,
it learns a prior over physical interactions that can be searched
using either gradient-based LNO or sampling-based optimization.
Unlike direct action-space search, which can propose out-of-distribution
actions and exploit world-model errors, searching this generative prior
biases planning toward plausible interaction trajectories.
Our experiments show that noise-space planning substantially
outperforms action-space optimization even when both use the same
world model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2611.08338v1/arch_faithful_v2.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/190;" width="357" height="190"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GPWM architecture.<span id="S3.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Noisy per-particle tokens, which embed
displacement, actuator motion, geometry, physical parameters, and material,
pass through a multi-resolution DiT. PointNet++ layers pool particles into
per-object anchors on the way down and interpolate back on the way up, and
long skips connect matching levels. Each block (right) applies temporal
attention, 3D relative spatial attention, and pointwise feed-forward layers,
modulated by AdaLN-Zero from the per-frame noise level <math id="S3.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, and the network
outputs clean future displacements.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formulate world modeling as conditional generation of 3D scene
trajectories. A scene contains <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> tracked particles with positions
<math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> at frame <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, grouped into objects,
including <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> rigid bodies. We assume particle correspondences and object
assignments are known. Given <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> observed frames <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{0:C-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{0:C-1}</annotation></semantics></math>,
GPWM models a distribution over the next <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> frames, optionally conditioned
on material properties and prescribed actuator motion.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPWM represents motion through particle displacements and rigid-body
transformations (Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Particle and Rigid-Body Representation ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), processed by an object-aware,
multi-resolution spatio-temporal transformer (Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Multi-Resolution Spatio-Temporal Transformer ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).
We train the model with flow matching and diffusion forcing
(Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Flow Matching with Diffusion Forcing ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) and use a streaming denoising schedule to generate
trajectories beyond the training window (Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Streaming Long-Horizon Generation ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>).
For planning, task-specific models jointly generate actuator and object
trajectories, allowing rewards on object outcomes to guide actuator motion
(Section <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Particle and Rigid-Body Representation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPWM represents scene motion through particle displacements and rigid-body
transformations. The generative variables reflect each component’s physical
structure, while particle geometry provides a shared representation for
modeling interactions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Particle representation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the number of particles represented by individual displacement
variables, with positions <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{t}^{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{t}^{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Their frame-to-frame displacements are
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{P}_{t}^{p}=\mathbf{P}_{t+1}^{p}-\mathbf{P}_{t}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{P}_{t}^{p}=\mathbf{P}_{t+1}^{p}-\mathbf{P}_{t}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and the clean future trajectory is <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}=[\Delta\mathbf{P}_{C-1}^{p},\ldots,\Delta\mathbf{P}_{C+F-2}^{p}]\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times N_{p}\times 3}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}=[\Delta\mathbf{P}_{C-1}^{p},\ldots,\Delta\mathbf{P}_{C+F-2}^{p}]\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times N_{p}\times 3}.</annotation></semantics></math>
Future positions are recovered by accumulating these displacements from the
last observed frame. This makes the motion targets invariant to global
translation. Where available, we condition on material type and physical
parameters: Young’s modulus <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>, Poisson’s ratio <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math>, and density <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>.
Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Multi-Resolution Spatio-Temporal Transformer ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> describes how motion, geometry, and conditioning
information are embedded into particle tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Rigid-body representation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each rigid body <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is represented by both a pose token and particle tokens. The pose token encodes its frame-to-frame transformation, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{q}_{k}^{t}=[\Delta\mathbf{t}_{k}^{t},\Delta\mathbf{r}_{k}^{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{9}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐭</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>9</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{q}_{k}^{t}=[\Delta\mathbf{t}_{k}^{t},\Delta\mathbf{r}_{k}^{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{9},</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{t}_{k}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐭</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{t}_{k}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is a translation increment and
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{r}_{k}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{r}_{k}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the relative
rotation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
The clean future rigid-body trajectory is
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}_{0}=[\Delta\mathbf{q}^{C-1},\ldots,\Delta\mathbf{q}^{C+F-2}]\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times K\times 9}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐪</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐪</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}_{0}=[\Delta\mathbf{q}^{C-1},\ldots,\Delta\mathbf{q}^{C+F-2}]\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times K\times 9}.</annotation></semantics></math>
We recover future poses from the last observed pose by accumulating
translations and composing the rotation matrices decoded from these
increments. Applying each pose to fixed body-frame particles preserves rigid shape by construction. These particles do not receive their own noise; they move with the noisy pose of their rigid body. Pose and particle trajectories are denoised jointly by the multi-resolution spatio-temporal transformer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Actuator conditioning.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We represent actuator commands using the same geometric variables as scene
motion: prescribed particle displacements <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{i}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{i}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math> or rigid-body
transformations. Rods, grippers, and articulated hands are therefore described
through the motion of their physical components. When future actuator motion
is supplied, GPWM conditions on it to generate the resulting object
trajectories. For planning, task-specific models jointly generate actuator and
object trajectories, allowing rewards on future object configurations to guide
actuator motion (Section <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Multi-Resolution Spatio-Temporal Transformer</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Direct attention over all particles and frames is prohibitively expensive for
scenes containing thousands of particles. We therefore use a multi-resolution
architecture that progressively compresses dense particles into a small set of
anchor tokens, performs most global interaction modeling at coarse resolution,
and propagates the resulting features back to the original particles (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Particle embeddings.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each particle <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> at frame <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is embedded as</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{i}^{t}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left([\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t},\,\mathbf{g}_{i}^{t},\,\bm{\phi}_{i},\,\mathbf{a}_{i}^{t}]\right)+\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.371em;" width="2.371em"><mi>MLP</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{i}^{t}=\mathrm{MLP}\!\left([\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t},\,\mathbf{g}_{i}^{t},\,\bm{\phi}_{i},\,\mathbf{a}_{i}^{t}]\right)+\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is its frame-to-frame displacement,
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{i}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{i}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math> encodes its displacement from its initial position together
with its absolute height,
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\phi}_{i}=[\log_{10}E_{i},\nu_{i},\rho_{i}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\phi}_{i}=[\log_{10}E_{i},\nu_{i},\rho_{i}]</annotation></semantics></math> contains available physical
parameters, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}_{m_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a learned embedding of material type
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. For context frames, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is observed; for future
frames, it is the corresponding noisy generative variable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-resolution particle hierarchy.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Particle tokens remain attached to physical particles at every resolution.
Coarse anchors are selected by farthest-point sampling (FPS) within each object
from the initial geometry. PointNet++-style layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2017</a>)</cite>
transfer information between resolutions. During downsampling, each anchor
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> aggregates features from a neighborhood within the same object.
Suppressing feature projections, normalization, and noise-dependent gates,
this aggregation is written schematically as</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{a}^{t}=\max_{j\in\mathcal{N}(a,t)}\mathrm{MLP}\!\left([\mathbf{h}_{j}^{t},\,\mathbf{h}_{j}^{t}-\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t},\,\mathbf{p}_{j}^{t}-\mathbf{p}_{a}^{t}]\right),\qquad\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t}+\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{a}^{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐡</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.371em;" width="2.371em"><mi>MLP</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐡</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{a}^{t}=\max_{j\in\mathcal{N}(a,t)}\mathrm{MLP}\!\left([\mathbf{h}_{j}^{t},\,\mathbf{h}_{j}^{t}-\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t},\,\mathbf{p}_{j}^{t}-\mathbf{p}_{a}^{t}]\right),\qquad\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t}+\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{a}^{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">During upsampling, coarse features are projected to the finer feature width
and interpolated back to finer particles using inverse-distance weighting,</p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{i}^{t}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{N}(i,t)}w_{ia}\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t},\qquad w_{ia}=\frac{(\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}-\mathbf{p}_{a}^{t}\|+\epsilon)^{-1}}{\sum_{b\in\mathcal{N}(i,t)}(\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}-\mathbf{p}_{b}^{t}\|+\epsilon)^{-1}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{i}^{t}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{N}(i,t)}w_{ia}\mathbf{h}_{a}^{t},\qquad w_{ia}=\frac{(\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}-\mathbf{p}_{a}^{t}\|+\epsilon)^{-1}}{\sum_{b\in\mathcal{N}(i,t)}(\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{t}-\mathbf{p}_{b}^{t}\|+\epsilon)^{-1}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> handles coincident points. The interpolated features are
fused with the corresponding encoder features through a gated MLP.
Neighborhoods are recomputed at each frame from particle positions obtained by
integrating the current noisy displacement trajectory. Anchor identities
remain fixed throughout the temporal window while their positions evolve.
Feature width increases as particle token count decreases, and most
transformer blocks operate at coarse resolutions. Rigid-body pose tokens are
retained at every resolution and participate in attention alongside particle
tokens. Linear projections change their feature width between resolutions
without pooling them.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Factorized spatio-temporal attention.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At each resolution, transformer blocks factorize attention into temporal and
spatial stages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arnab et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Temporal attention operates along each
token trajectory within the denoising window, while spatial attention connects
tokens within each frame. At
full resolution, spatial attention is restricted within each object; at
coarser resolutions, it spans the entire scene, allowing the model to capture
interactions between objects and actuators. Each attention stage is followed
by a feed-forward network, and blocks are modulated with
adaLN-Zero <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles &amp; Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> using the frame-specific noise level.
Encoder and decoder stages are connected by Hunyuan-DiT-style long
skips <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, preserving fine-scale information across the
multi-resolution hierarchy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Relative 3D geometry.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Particle inputs encode displacement from the initial position, and PointNet++
aggregation uses offsets relative to each anchor. Spatial attention applies
rotary position embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heo et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to the 3D coordinates of
particle and pose tokens. Absolute height is retained to represent vertical
position relative to the ground plane.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Flow Matching with Diffusion Forcing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train GPWM with flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and diffusion
forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Rather than assigning a single noise level
to the entire future trajectory, diffusion forcing samples an independent
noise level <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{t}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{t}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> for each future frame, collected in
<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{F})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝝉</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{F})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We normalize particle displacements and rigid-body increments before adding
noise. In this section, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> denote these normalized
trajectories. For the particle and rigid-body trajectories, respectively,</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{\bm{\tau}}^{t}=(1-\tau_{t})\mathbf{x}_{0}^{t}+\tau_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{x}^{t},\qquad\mathbf{y}_{\bm{\tau}}^{t}=(1-\tau_{t})\mathbf{y}_{0}^{t}+\tau_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{y}^{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{\bm{\tau}}^{t}=(1-\tau_{t})\mathbf{x}_{0}^{t}+\tau_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{x}^{t},\qquad\mathbf{y}_{\bm{\tau}}^{t}=(1-\tau_{t})\mathbf{y}_{0}^{t}+\tau_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{y}^{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where
<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\epsilon}_{x}^{t},\bm{\epsilon}_{y}^{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\epsilon}_{x}^{t},\bm{\epsilon}_{y}^{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus different future frames can be presented to the model at different stages
of the generative process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; He (2026)</a></cite>, we use an endpoint parameterization: rather than
predicting the flow velocity directly, the network predicts the clean particle
and rigid-body trajectories,</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>

properties and action conditioning. The flow field used for sampling is
recovered from the noisy state and predicted clean endpoint. We do not reweight this objective in velocity space and instead directly optimize</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> balances the particle and rigid-body terms. No auxiliary
physics-based losses are used.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Streaming Long-Horizon Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Independent per-frame noise levels allow different future frames to occupy
different stages of denoising at inference time. Following diffusion
forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we use a staggered denoising schedule:
near-future frames are progressively resolved, while farther-future frames
remain at higher noise levels and continue to be revised. Once the earliest
frames are fully denoised, they are committed, the prediction window
advances, and fresh Gaussian noise is appended at the far end of the horizon.
Repeating this process allows GPWM to generate trajectories beyond the
<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math>-frame training horizon while keeping the model’s temporal window fixed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Planning with Generative Interaction Priors</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Planning uses task-specific GPWM models (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 World Models ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>).
GPWM supports planning in either action space or the latent
space of its generative model. In action-space planning, candidate
actuator trajectories are evaluated using the action-conditioned
world model. Alternatively, by jointly generating actuator and
passive-object motion, GPWM learns a prior over physical
interactions that enables planning directly in latent noise space.
This biases search toward actuator–object trajectories represented
by the learned distribution, rather than unconstrained action
sequences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We specify planning objectives through a differentiable reward on
the desired final configuration of passive objects. With the world
model frozen, we optimize the initial Gaussian noise through
<em id="S3.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent noise optimization</em> (LNO)
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eyring et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ben-Hamu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karunratanakul et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Let <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the initial noise for an <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>-frame rollout
and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{1:H}(\mathbf{z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{1:H}(\mathbf{z})</annotation></semantics></math> the generated scene
trajectory, reconstructed in physical coordinates by denormalizing
and integrating predicted motion. With <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{\mathrm{pass}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>pass</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{\mathrm{pass}}</annotation></semantics></math>
selecting the passive-object configuration, LNO performs</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}\leftarrow\mathbf{z}+\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}r\!\left(\Pi_{\mathrm{pass}}(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{H}(\mathbf{z}))\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝐳</mi></msub><mpadded style="width:0.309em;" width="0.309em"><mi>r</mi></mpadded></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>pass</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}\leftarrow\mathbf{z}+\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}r\!\left(\Pi_{\mathrm{pass}}(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{H}(\mathbf{z}))\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> is the guidance step size.
As a gradient-free alternative, we also apply the cross-entropy
method (CEM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rubinstein, 1999</a>)</cite> in the same latent noise space, iteratively sampling
and selecting noise vectors according to their predicted terminal
rewards.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For horizons <math id="S3.SS5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H&gt;F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H&gt;F</annotation></semantics></math>, we use the streaming generation procedure
of Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Streaming Long-Horizon Generation ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>. In LNO, gradients propagate through
successive generation windows, allowing terminal object-space
rewards to guide earlier actuator motion. The actuator component
of the optimized joint trajectory defines the resulting plan,
which is executed open-loop in simulation
(Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>).
Further details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" title="Noise CEM. ‣ E.3 Planners ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span> Dataset</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>, a dataset of 25.5 million simulated training frames
spanning rigid objects, elastic and elastoplastic solids, granular materials,
and cloth. Its six domains cover passive dynamics and robotic
manipulation with rods, parallel-jaw grippers, and articulated hands
(Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A ParticleWorlds Dataset Details ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). Scenes range from isolated objects to cluttered
environments, with representations containing 256–12,000 particles and
geometries including irregular objects and garments from ten categories. This
breadth supports both domain-specific models and a unified world model
trained across materials and robot embodiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We generate trajectories for falling objects, deformable dragging,
garment manipulation, dexterous manipulation, rod and gripper pushing, and
pick-and-place <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. To combine
these sources, we convert simulator outputs into the common particle
representation of Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Particle and Rigid-Body Representation ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, preserving particle
identities and object membership over time. Deformable bodies use tracked
material or mesh points; rigid bodies and actuator links use fixed surface
samples transformed by their recorded poses. Dataset sources, generation
procedures, and split definitions are detailed in
Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A ParticleWorlds Dataset Details ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate GPWM along three dimensions:
<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) prediction</span> across rigid, deformable, granular, and cloth dynamics;
<span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) generalization</span> across geometry, physical properties, scene
complexity, and rollout horizon, including joint training across heterogeneous
regimes; and <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3) contact-rich planning</span> from sparse object-space
rewards.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare against four learned 3D dynamics models:
GNS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, a graph-based particle simulator;
PGND <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a hybrid particle–grid model;
PointWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, a point-cloud world model; and
PhysCtrl <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, a generative model of physical dynamics.
Each is evaluated where its conditioning applies: PhysCtrl on all domains,
GNS on non-action-conditioned domains, PointWorld on robot-actuated domains, and PGND on
robot-actuated domains and Dragging. We report domain-specific GPWM models (<span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Specialist</span>) for
direct comparison and a single <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unified</span> model trained across all
domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental setup.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Unless stated otherwise, GPWM observes four context frames and predicts
16 future frames per window. Predictions are rolled forward to the end of each
trajectory, up to 898 frames for Garment Folding (over <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="55\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>55</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">55\times</annotation></semantics></math> the
prediction window). Recorded actuator motion is provided for action-conditioned tasks;
passive tasks require no action input. All methods use the same evaluation
trajectories and available actuator conditioning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For physical prediction, we report mean Euclidean position error
(mm, <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>) over passive-object particles, averaging over particles and
frames and then equally across trajectories. We evaluate one sample from
GPWM. Because physical interactions can be multimodal, error against a
single recorded future does not fully capture physical plausibility; we
therefore provide extensive qualitative rollouts on our
<a href="https://robertren1122.github.io/gpwm/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a>. For cloth, we report symmetric Chamfer distance
(<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>). Planning is instead evaluated by task progress toward the goal
(Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Prediction across Physical Regimes</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ State-of-the-art prediction across diverse physics. ‣ 5.1 Prediction across Physical Regimes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares prediction across six
physical settings spanning rigid, deformable, granular, and cloth dynamics.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">State-of-the-art prediction across diverse physics.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPWM outperforms the strongest applicable baseline in all six settings,
reducing error by <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6–67%</span> (31% on average) with the better of its
specialist and unified models (Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ State-of-the-art prediction across diverse physics. ‣ 5.1 Prediction across Physical Regimes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
The gains span qualitatively different dynamics: error decreases from 53.0 to 40.0 mm on Free Fall, 7.8 to 6.1 mm on Dragging, and 23.9 to 13.3 mm on Pushing.
Together, these results show that the same generative particle formulation
achieves strong prediction accuracy across substantially different physical
regimes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S5.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Prediction across diverse physical settings.<span id="S5.T1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">

(Specialist) are trained separately for each setting; Ours (Unified) uses a
single model across heterogeneous settings. Graph/grid-based denotes GNS or
PGND, depending on the setting. –: not applicable. <sup id="S5.T1.6.1.1" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>Garment Folding reports symmetric Chamfer distance averaged over 898 predicted frames on 20 test trajectories.</span></span></figcaption>
