<td id="S5.T1.7.6.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 3.0pt;"><span id="S5.T1.7.6.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">11.1</span></td>
<td id="S5.T1.7.6.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 3.0pt;"><span id="S5.T1.7.6.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline" style="font-size:90%;">22.6</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">One model across heterogeneous physics.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A single Unified GPWM spans heterogeneous materials, interactions, and
actuator embodiments within one set of weights. It outperforms all evaluated
prior methods on five of the six settings, and achieves
the best overall performance on Dragging and Pick and Place, improving even over the
GPWM specialists (Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ State-of-the-art prediction across diverse physics. ‣ 5.1 Prediction across Physical Regimes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Domain-specific specialists remain
more accurate on the other settings, revealing a specialization gap while
demonstrating that substantially different physical regimes can be captured
within a single model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Generalization across Geometry and Physics</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct controlled generalization experiments in the Free Fall setting,
where geometry, object count, and material properties can be varied
independently. Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ GPWM generalizes to unseen shapes and larger scenes. ‣ 5.2 Generalization across Geometry and Physics ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> evaluates GPWM as
each factor moves beyond the training distribution. GPWM achieves the
lowest prediction error across all generalization conditions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GPWM generalizes to unseen shapes and larger scenes.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Free Fall training scenes contain one to four objects. At test time, we
introduce unseen geometries and increase scene complexity to five to seven
objects, reaching 7,168 particles. Unseen shapes increase specialist error
by less than 7%, while combining unseen shapes with larger scenes raises
error only from 37.5 to 45.2 mm. In contrast, PhysCtrl increases from
48.5 to 120.9 mm. The Unified model is also stable across these shifts and ranks second in all four shape and object-count conditions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Generalization on Free Fall.<span id="S5.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Mean particle position error
in millimeters (<math id="S5.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>). Training uses one to four objects per scene.
Stiffness values are seen (10, 100, 1,000 kPa) or unseen within the training
range (30, 300 kPa). Material types are weighted equally.</span></span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GPWM generalizes to unseen material stiffness.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next vary Young’s modulus from 10 kPa to 1 MPa, covering values seen during
training and unseen values within the training range.
Models receive the material parameters and initial observations for each
simulation. GPWM’s error rises by less than 2 mm on unseen values (47.3 to
48.9 mm) while remaining below the strongest baseline. This demonstrates robust
prediction under interpolation of material stiffness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GPWM generalizes to objects reconstructed from images.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also test GPWM on previously unseen object geometries reconstructed
from single RGB images (Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ GPWM generalizes to objects reconstructed from images. ‣ 5.2 Generalization across Geometry and Physics ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). SAM 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carion et al., 2025</a>)</cite>
segments the objects, SAM 3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">SAM 3D Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite> reconstructs their meshes, and
MoGe-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> estimates their metric scene placement. We sample surface
particles from the reconstructed meshes, assign physical properties, and use
the Free Fall specialist to predict their dynamics. The resulting trajectories
are rendered back into the scene, demonstrating that GPWM can operate
on reconstructed real-world geometry rather than only simulator-native assets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/drop_from_image.png" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/195;" width="476" height="195" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Predictions from a single image.<span id="S5.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Each row shows the input
with the reconstructed objects outlined, their particles, and the predicted
motion. Top, a tower of a toy car (elastic, 1 MPa), a pepper (sand,
100 kPa), a lemon (plasticine, 100 kPa), and a ball (elastic, 100 kPa).
Bottom, an elastic ball (10 kPa) dropped onto a sand or a plasticine castle
(100 kPa).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Planning with Generative Interaction Priors</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPWM supports two approaches to model-based planning.
In <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">action-space planning</em>, candidate actuator trajectories are evaluated
using an action-conditioned world model. However, searching unconstrained
action sequences presents two challenges: complex contact-rich behaviors
are difficult to discover without a suitable action proposal policy, and
optimization may exploit prediction errors by selecting actions outside
the model’s training distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPWM offers an alternative: by jointly generating actuator and
passive-object trajectories, it learns a <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generative prior over physical
interactions</em>. Planning can then search the model’s latent noise rather
than raw actuator commands, biasing optimization toward plausible
actuator–object trajectories. We optimize this noise using either
gradient-based latent noise optimization (LNO)
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eyring et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ben-Hamu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karunratanakul et al., 2024</a>)</cite>
or gradient-free sampling. In LNO, a differentiable terminal reward on the
passive-object configuration is backpropagated through the generated
trajectory to the initial noise (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare action-
and noise-space planning on three contact-rich tasks, using task-specific
world models and rewards defined solely on desired object outcomes
(Fig. <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Planning methods. ‣ 5.3 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). All generated actuator trajectories are executed
<span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">open-loop in simulation</span>, testing whether plans optimized through
the learned dynamics succeed under the underlying simulator.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tasks and metrics.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate three tasks requiring different contact strategies.
<span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pushing</span> requires a rod to reposition around a rigid block before
pushing it toward a target over 60 steps.
<span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pile Manipulation</span> requires a paddle to move a granular pile toward
a target over 150 steps, typically through multiple pushes.
<span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Picking</span> requires establishing a stable grasp and lifting an object
to a target over 60 steps. We evaluate five objects of different shapes
and sizes (milk carton, peanut-butter jar, soda can, pasta box, and water
bottle), each with five targets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task progress</em>, defined as the fraction of the initial
object-to-target distance closed by the end of the episode. Performance is
measured across planning budgets of up to 100 s for Pushing and 200 s
for Pile Manipulation and Picking, on a single L40S GPU. Additional task
details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Planning Tasks ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Planning methods.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Noise-space planning.</em>
<span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Latent Noise Optimization (LNO)</span> optimizes the initial Gaussian noise by backpropagating the terminal
reward through the generated trajectory. As a gradient-free alternative,
<em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Noise CEM</em> applies the cross-entropy method in the same latent space:
each iteration samples candidate noise vectors, generates and evaluates
their trajectories, and refits the sampling distribution to the
highest-reward candidates. Both methods exploit the learned joint distribution
over actuator and object motion. Generated actuator trajectories are
executed using a simple tracking controller.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Action-space planning.</em>
<em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Action CEM</em> instead optimizes raw per-frame end-effector
displacements, evaluating each candidate using an action-conditioned
world model. We apply Action CEM to both GPWM and
PointWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Crucially, action-space and
noise-space planning use the <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">same GPWM checkpoint</em>, isolating
the effect of the search space rather than differences in model accuracy.
We vary planning budgets through the number of samples, optimization
iterations, or CEM rounds. Implementation details are provided in
Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Planners ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2611.08338v1/task_progress_planning.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/165;" width="476" height="165"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Planning performance.<span id="S5.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Task progress versus planning budget, measured after open-loop execution
in simulation. Results are averaged over 50 scenarios for Pushing and
Pile Manipulation and 25 problems for Picking. Reported values are
interpolated at each task’s planning budget (dashed lines).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure" style="width:38%;"><img src="2611.08338v1/guidance.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:181/202;" width="181" height="202" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Planning with a generative interaction prior.<span id="S5.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Latent noise optimization guides a frozen GPWM toward an object-space
goal (green <math id="S5.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>). When a wall blocks the direct path, the generated
actuator trajectory lifts the object over it.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generative interaction priors enable contact-rich planning.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Planning methods. ‣ 5.3 Planning with Generative Interaction Priors ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that searching GPWM’s
noise space substantially outperforms direct action-space optimization,
even when both use the same world model. On Pushing and Picking,
noise-space planners achieve 0.48–0.57 and 0.40–0.56 task progress,
respectively, while action-space planners remain at or below 0.01.
These tasks require discovering structured sequences of contact:
repositioning the rod before pushing, or establishing a grasp before
lifting. Such behaviors are unlikely to emerge from random action
proposals, whereas GPWM’s learned interaction prior provides
plausible trajectories that can be steered toward the goal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Pile Manipulation presents a different regime: even random paddle
contacts can produce task progress, making action-space search more
competitive. Nevertheless, noise-space planning achieves 0.21–0.23
task progress, compared with 0.19 for the strongest action-space baseline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond discovering effective contacts, the generative prior also reduces
the risk of exploiting world-model errors. Direct action optimization can
select out-of-distribution trajectories that appear successful under the
learned dynamics but fail when executed in simulation, as illustrated
by Picking (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a>). Noise-space optimization instead
searches through the model’s learned distribution of interactions,
favoring actuator motions whose predicted effects are more likely to
transfer to the underlying simulator.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results demonstrate that <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">accurate dynamics prediction
alone is insufficient for effective contact-rich planning</em>: the learned
distribution of actuator–object interactions provides a powerful
search prior, enabling object-space goals to be translated into actuator
trajectories without reference demonstrations or goal-specific policies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Additional qualitative results, including baseline comparisons,
generalization to real-world images, and planning examples, are available
on our <a href="https://robertren1122.github.io/gpwm/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Limitations and Future Directions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several limitations remain. First, GPWM assumes access to complete,
temporally tracked 3D scene state. Our experiments therefore isolate physical
prediction from perception and do not address recovering persistent particles
and object identities from raw visual observations. An important next step is
to integrate 3D reconstruction and tracking, ultimately learning physical world
models directly from RGB or RGB-D video.
Second, although a single Unified GPWM can model heterogeneous physical
regimes within one set of weights, it still trails domain-specific
models on some settings. This specialization gap suggests interference
between heterogeneous dynamics and motivates better data balancing, better-matched point density across domains,
domain-aware routing or mixture-of-experts architectures, and increased model
capacity as the diversity of physical experience grows.
Finally, latent noise optimization requires differentiating through the full
generative process and, for long-horizon tasks, through multiple streaming
windows. Its computational cost therefore grows with planning horizon and
currently limits rapid online control. Faster generative parameterizations,
including flow maps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, could substantially reduce the cost
of long-horizon reward-guided planning, an exciting direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced GPWM, a generative 3D particle world-modeling framework for
physical prediction and contact-rich planning. Across rigid, deformable,
granular, and cloth dynamics, domain-specific GPWM models outperform prior
learned dynamics approaches, while a single Unified model demonstrates that
heterogeneous physical regimes can be modeled within one set of weights.
Flow matching with diffusion forcing enables stable auto-regressive generation far beyond
the training horizon, including coherent deformable-object prediction for more
than <math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="55\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>55</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">55\times</annotation></semantics></math> the trained prediction window. Beyond prediction, GPWM learns a generative prior over coupled
actuator–object motion that enables contact-rich planning from object-space
goals. Searching this learned interaction prior substantially outperforms
direct action-space optimization, even when using the same world model. Together, these results establish
generative particle world models as a common framework for long-horizon
physical prediction and goal-directed interaction in 3D.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span><span id="A1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span> Dataset Details</h2>

<figure id="A1.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/dataset_examples.png" id="A1.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:419/552;" width="419" height="552" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A1.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Examples from the <span id="A1.F6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span> domains.<span id="A1.F6.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Each row shows one
recorded episode at four moments, labeled with the time since its first
frame; Pushing has one row for each of its two sources. From the top, four objects of three materials fall onto the table, a
piggy bank is lifted by a patch on its back and released, two grippers fold a
shirt, a rod pushes a block, a gripper pushes an object, a gripper picks up an
object from a cluttered table and places it, and a hand turns a cube. Actuated
parts are orange, and objects keep the colors of their meshes where
available. Rigid bodies are drawn with extra points that follow their
recorded poses, denser than the points the model receives. Rod Pushing
records no time step, so its panels give frame indices.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A1.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="A1.T3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of <span id="A1.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span>.<span id="A1.T3.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Pushing combines rod and gripper recordings, and Pick and Place combines
single-object and cluttered recordings. Frame
counts refer to usable training episodes at each domain’s training
sampling rate, including recorded settling frames.</span></span></figcaption>

<td id="A1.T3.6.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Rigid</span></td>
<td id="A1.T3.6.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Gripper</span></td>
<td id="A1.T3.6.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.6.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">7,257,150</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T3.6.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T3.6.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.7.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Dexterous Hands</span></td>
<td id="A1.T3.6.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Rigid</span></td>
<td id="A1.T3.6.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Articulated hand</span></td>
<td id="A1.T3.6.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.7.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">5,679,049</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T3.6.8" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T3.6.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;" colspan="3"><span id="A1.T3.6.8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Total</span></td>
<td id="A1.T3.6.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.35pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T3.6.8.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">25,463,677</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Domains and counting convention.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The six domains in Table <a href="#A1.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix A ParticleWorlds Dataset Details ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> group eight sources:
Pushing combines rod and gripper pushing, and Pick and Place combines
single-object and cluttered recordings.
The corpus contains 267,864 usable training episodes and 25,463,677
scene frames, counted once at each loader’s temporal rate, including
recorded settling prefixes. Counts exclude test episodes and do not multiply
frames by overlapping windows, repeated training draws, or particle counts.
Rod and gripper pushing contribute 3,706,040 and 2,252,357 frames,
and single-object and cluttered Pick and Place contribute 1,690,120 and
5,567,030 frames, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generation and source trajectories.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Free Fall and Dragging.</span> We generate both domains with the Genesis material-point
solver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Genesis Authors, 2024</a>)</cite>. Falling scenes contain one to four objects with
1,024 material points each and span elastic recovery, permanent deformation,
and granular rearrangement. Dragging uses elastic and elastoplastic objects:
prescribed velocities drive a persistent patch of material points through
pull, hold, and release events. Falling episodes contain 49 recorded states;
dragging episodes contain 49, 81, or 113 states, depending on the number of
events, with a recorded interval of 0.0417 seconds.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Garment Folding.</span>
We generate scripted garment manipulation with two grippers in
SIM1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. After filtering, the domain covers 988 garments from ten
categories. Each clip contains approximately 900 states at 30 Hz. The representation uses
a persistent farthest-point subset of the garment mesh with 8 mm spacing,
capped at 10,000 cloth points, together with 1,000 points per gripper.
The same garment subset is used across frames and clips. These are
numerically screened manipulation trajectories, not verified successful folds.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rigid manipulation.</span>
Pushing has two sources. Rod Pushing uses our recordings of scripted
rod motion against a block,
with 40 states and 256 points per episode. Gripper Pushing uses our
reinforcement-learning policy recordings of successful object pushes.
Pick and Place recordings come from SkillWeaver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Single-object Pick and Place combines recordings of four policies for
picking, picking convex objects, bringing objects upright, and placing held
objects. Its cluttered counterpart includes the target and surrounding
objects, which may move or remain still. For Dexterous Hands, we
generate trajectories from five teacher policies in Genesis using XHand1
and Sharpa hands for object rotation, reorientation, and screwdriver turning.
The rigid gripper and hand recordings are consumed at 20 Hz.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Inputs, targets, and physical properties.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Action-conditioned prediction receives scene history and the future motion
of rigid actuator links, and predicts passive-object dynamics. Cluttered
Pick and Place includes the surrounding objects in the prediction target.
Dragging instead supplies commanded material-point velocities, together
with indicators distinguishing a stationary hold from a release. These
commands need not equal the achieved motion: the target includes every
material point, including the driven patch. Passive falling scenes have no
action input. Recorded physical properties are supplied where available.
The MPM domain varies stiffness over three values while fixing Poisson’s
ratio and density; garment parameters and the randomized mass and friction
of Gripper Pushing and Dexterous Hands are not recorded for conditioning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Splits and coverage.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The release holds out geometries for Free Fall, Dragging,
single-object Pick and Place, and Dexterous Hands, and splits
Garment Folding by garment identity. Cluttered Pick and Place uses held-out
scenes. Rod Pushing tests new
trajectories on the same geometry. Gripper Pushing holds out objects.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Quality control.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Source-specific screening removes numerical failures and conspicuous
simulation artifacts. MPM checks cover unsettled starts, wall interactions,
collapse, and persistent fragmentation during dragging; cloth clips undergo
numerical screening. Rigid-object audits detect table penetration, abrupt
motion, excessive hand–object overlap, and other failures, with exclusion
manifests recording rejected episodes and reasons. We also check pose and
surface-template reconstruction against recorded particles. Screening reduces
artifacts but does not establish solver convergence.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Model, Training, and Baseline Details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Architecture</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every reported model uses the multi-resolution network of
Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Multi-Resolution Spatio-Temporal Transformer ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, with the sizes in Table <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ B.1 Architecture ‣ Appendix B Model, Training, and Baseline Details ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
The hierarchy has four levels. The first holds every particle. The second keeps,
per object, 256 anchors for elastic, plasticine, and sand objects, 128 for rigid
bodies and robot links, and 512 for cloth. The third and fourth levels divide
these counts by 4 and then by 2, so a Free Fall object of 1,024 particles is
represented by 256, 64, and 32 anchors. Downsampling aggregates the 8 nearest
tokens of each anchor within its object, and upsampling interpolates from the 3
nearest anchors. From the third level on, each block also carries one object’s worth of
register tokens. Temporal attention is bidirectional within the window in every reported
model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span><span id="A2.T4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Network sizes.</span> The six specialists share one configuration.
Levels run from the particles (first) to the coarsest anchors (fourth).</figcaption>
<table id="A2.T4.7" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A2.T4.7.1" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A2.T4.7.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A2.T4.7.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Unified</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T4.7.2" class="ltx_tr">

</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Training</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each specialist is trained on one domain. The unified model is trained on
all of them, and every batch comes from one domain drawn with equal probability.
A training window has 4 context frames and 16 future frames. Particle displacements and rigid-body increments are normalized
per domain by the 99th percentile of their per-frame magnitude, separately
in the horizontal plane and along the vertical axis.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Future frames are noised with diffusion forcing. In 60% of the windows every future frame draws its own noise level uniformly, and in the other 40% the noise level rises linearly along the window, so nearer frames are less noisy than farther ones, as during streaming inference. Context frames stay clean, except
the history of passive objects receives Gaussian jitter with a standard
deviation of 0.05 in normalized units, which imitates the error of predicted
context during rollouts. The network predicts the clean trajectories, and the
particle and rigid-body terms of the loss are weighted equally (<math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=1</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">All GPWM models are trained with Muon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> on the weight matrices (learning rate <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>,
with the update scaled to match AdamW’s RMS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) and AdamW on all remaining parameters
(learning rate <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.999</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.999</annotation></semantics></math>), with decoupled weight decay
of <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> for both. Both learning rates follow a 5,000-step linear warmup and a
cosine decay to 1% of their peak value. We clip gradients to a global norm of <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>,
keep an exponential moving average of the weights with decay <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9999</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9999</annotation></semantics></math>, and train in
bf16 mixed precision. We train each specialist on two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs for 200k iterations,
and the unified model on four for 600k iterations. Note that while the unified model has seen more training iterations, these update steps are split across 6 domains. So the unified model gets only 100k iterations per domain, half the amount that the specialist models see.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each baseline is trained per domain on the same training episodes and
evaluated on the same test clips, with the same given frames and actuator
motion as our model unless noted.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">PhysCtrl <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build on the authors’ implementation and keep its spatiotemporal transformer and its diffusion objective. We scale it to about 100 M parameters (8 blocks with hidden size 640) and train it from scratch on our data. The model receives the same history of 4 observed frames as ours, instead of the single frame it was designed for, predicts the same 16 frames per window, and processes every particle of the scene without subsampling.
<br class="ltx_break">PhysCtrl takes an action as regions of particles and the motion applied to each region. We cluster the actuator’s particles by position into a few regions, with farthest point sampling choosing the region centers. The action is then given region by region. For every region and every predicted frame, the model receives two conditioning tokens, the position of the region’s center and the region’s average displacement in that frame. These tokens join the spatial attention of every frame, so every particle can attend to them. We do not give PhysCtrl rigid-body poses, since its interface does not support them. As for our model, the actuator’s future motion is an input and is never predicted.
<br class="ltx_break">All objects share a single point cloud, and the spatial attention is all-to-all over the particles of each frame. Through PhysCtrl’s
per-particle conditioning path, each particle is also tagged with the object it belongs to and that object’s material parameters <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\log E,\nu,\log\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>ν</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\log E,\nu,\log\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">PointWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PointWorld is a deterministic point-cloud dynamics model with a PTv3 backbone. We
train it from scratch with its released code adapted to our setting: it
operates on complete 3D point clouds and is applied recurrently to produce the
autoregressive rollouts used in our evaluation. To match our 100 M-parameter
specialists, we use the released small variant with wider channels (about
100 M parameters), and train each run on the same episodes, splits, start frames
and number of action-conditioned training windows as our corresponding
specialist.
<br class="ltx_break">PointWorld voxel-downsamples each point cloud before its backbone, by default on a
<math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> mm grid; on several of our domains this discards much of the objects’
geometry, so we use a <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> mm grid instead, and at evaluation each surviving
point’s prediction is copied to the points merged into its voxel. We drop the
input features our data does not provide, such as color and surface normals:
each scene point carries only its positions over time and its distance to the
robot, and each actuator point its positions, velocity and acceleration. We
disable the training-time sphere crop, which removes scene points far from the
actuator, so the model sees the whole scene, and fit its normalization
statistics on <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> training windows of each domain. The released optimizer
and augmentations are otherwise unchanged.
<br class="ltx_break">PointWorld receives the actuator’s points at every frame and predicts only the
scene, the actuator’s future motion is an input and is never
predicted. It observes a single context frame, where our models receive <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>, and
we extend its prediction horizon from the released <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> frames to <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> to match
our models. For cloth, training windows are drawn with the same motion weighting
as our loader. Longer evaluation windows are rolled out autoregressively in
<math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math>-frame chunks, each anchored on the model’s own previous prediction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GNS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use GNS only for passive dynamics (Free Fall) where no actuator
drives the scene; it is not run on the action-conditioned settings where PGND serves as the graph/grid-based
baseline. We train it on the same episodes, splits, and start frames as our models, keeping the published
architecture: <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> message-passing steps, <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>128</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional latents and a <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.015" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.015</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.015</annotation></semantics></math> m connectivity radius. It is a
one-step model, so we roll it out autoregressively at every step to obtain a full-length prediction. GNS carries a
learned embedding of a discrete particle type plus a material channel that is hard-coded to one scalar. We widen
that channel to a per-particle vector and feed in each particle’s normalized material properties.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">PGND <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train PGND with <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> given and <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> predicted frames at each domain’s native frame rate, rolling the model out
one frame at a time with each prediction fed back as input. Its actuator representation needed the most change.
PGND either drives material with a sphere collider or shows the network a rigid <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>500</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500</annotation></semantics></math>-point gripper template posed
by the end-effector, so its fingers never articulate. We instead feed the recorded actuator points every frame so
finger motion is represented. The Dragging domain has no tool at all, since a patch of <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}100</annotation></semantics></math> material points is
driven by a commanded velocity, so there we use PGND’s sphere collider, placed on the patch at the start of each
drag and then moved only by the commanded velocity, independent of the material. PGND does not condition on physics
properties; on Dragging, where our model receives each object’s material, we give PGND the same information as
extra per-particle input channels. PGND simulates inside a fixed grid. Rather than excluding episodes that do not
fit, we enlarge the grid or rescale the scene so that every training episode fits, and for cluttered Pick and Place
we recenter a fixed <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.4\times 1.0\times 1.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1.4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.4\times 1.0\times 1.4</annotation></semantics></math> m grid on the gripper for each training window, freezing objects
that leave it. In every domain the network’s neighborhood radius covers the same <math id="A2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> cm as PGND’s released
recipes. Otherwise, we train PGND with the same episodes, splits, and start frames as our own loader, and match each
run to our corresponding specialist in gradient steps and windows per step.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Evaluation Protocol</h2>

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prediction protocol and metrics.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All baseline models are domain-specific specialists, as are the
GPWM models in the Specialist row of
Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ State-of-the-art prediction across diverse physics. ‣ 5.1 Prediction across Physical Regimes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The Unified row uses a single
model trained jointly across all six <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ParticleWorlds</span> domains. Methods are
evaluated on the same test trajectories with the same available actuator
conditioning. On action-conditioned tasks, recorded future actuator motion
is supplied throughout the rollout; passive-dynamics tasks require no action
conditioning. Predictions are fed back as context for subsequent windows.
For particle-tracked dynamics, we average Euclidean position error over
passive-object particles and predicted rollout frames, then average equally
across trajectories. Prescribed actuator motion is excluded from the error.
Cloth is evaluated using symmetric Chamfer distance, since particle
correspondence is not shared across all methods and surface geometry is the
quantity of interest.
Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Additional Prediction Results ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> shows predictions on every domain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Test sets.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Test sets. ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Protocol ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> lists the test clips behind each column. Every
rollout starts from 4 recorded frames and runs to the last recorded frame of its
clip, so horizons vary within a domain. A clip’s error is its mean over the
predicted frames and the passive particles, and a column averages clips with
equal weight. Actuator particles, which are given, are not scored.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span><span id="A3.T5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test clips.</span> The Held out column indicates how the test set differs from training.
Predicted frames give the range of rollout lengths.</figcaption>

<td id="A3.T5.7.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="A3.T5.7.8.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Garment Folding</span></td>
<td id="A3.T5.7.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="A3.T5.7.8.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">20</span></td>
<td id="A3.T5.7.8.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="A3.T5.7.8.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">garments</span></td>
<td id="A3.T5.7.8.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="A3.T5.7.8.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">898</span></td>
<td id="A3.T5.7.8.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="A3.T5.7.8.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1/30 s</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section shows test clips for every domain of
Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ State-of-the-art prediction across diverse physics. ‣ 5.1 Prediction across Physical Regimes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Every model rolls out from the same four
recorded frames with the same actuator motion. The error under each panel is the mean position error of the
predicted particles at that frame.</p>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Planning</h2>

<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Planning Tasks</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In every task an actuator must bring a passive object to a target within
a fixed number of steps. The reward is sparse and defined only on the
final frame: the negative distance from the object’s centroid to its
target. Each planner produces a single open-loop plan for the full
horizon inside its world model; the plan is then executed in the
task’s simulator from the same start state, and the simulator never
enters planning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A5.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1em;">
<li id="A5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pushing.</span> A rod pushes a rigid block toward a target on
a tabletop. Targets typically require the rod to move around the
block before pushing, so random rod motions rarely produce progress.
Horizon 60 steps (<math id="A5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> the model window), 50 scenarios, executed
in ManiSkill.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pile Manipulation.</span> A paddle moves the centroid of a
granular pile toward a target in the plane. World models are trained
on <math id="A5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> trajectories of 300 frames from a scripted policy that
randomly pushes and presses the pile. Horizon 150 steps
(<math id="A5.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="7.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>7.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> the model window), 50 scenarios, executed in Genesis.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Picking.</span> A parallel-jaw gripper must grasp a tabletop
object (milk carton, peanut-butter jar, soda can, pasta box, or water
bottle) and carry it to a target 15 cm above and up to 15 cm to the
side of its start (5 objects <math id="A5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 5 targets). Horizon 60 steps,
executed with a floating Franka hand in Isaac Lab.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A5.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ E.1 Planning Tasks ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> shows one scenario of each task and the
executed plan found by LNO.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F18" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/appendix_planning_tasks.png" id="A5.F18.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/259;" width="476" height="259" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F18.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 18</span>: </span><span id="A5.F18.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Planning tasks.<span id="A5.F18.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> One scenario per task: the initial
configuration with its target (top) and the outcome of the LNO plan executed
open-loop in the simulator (bottom). The rod moves around the block before
pushing it; the paddle sweeps part of the pile onto the target; the gripper
grasps the jar before carrying it to the target.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metric and budget.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task progress is <math id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(d_{0}-d_{T})/d_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(d_{0}-d_{T})/d_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> are the
object-to-target distances at the start and at the end of the executed
episode; it is averaged over scenarios. The planning budget is the
wall-clock time of the whole planning call on one L40S GPU. Each planner is run at a
ladder of settings (Table <a href="#A5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Scaling the planning budget. ‣ E.3 Planners ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), and the value
reported at a task’s budget is linearly interpolated between the two
settings that bracket it.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>World Models</h3>

<section id="A5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GPWM.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each task uses a task-specific GPWM (100M parameters, 200k training
steps) trained on that task’s data. During training, the actuator’s
given motion is withheld in a random half of the windows and replaced by
a learned token, so the model learns both to generate the actuator
jointly with the scene and to follow a given actuator motion. Planning
uses the same checkpoint in both modes: noise-space planners use the
generative mode, and Action CEM uses the action-conditioned mode, in
which the actuator’s motion is given as per-frame rigid displacements.
Rollouts over the full horizon use the streaming sampler of
Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Streaming Long-Horizon Generation ‣ 3 Method ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a> with 6 denoising steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">PointWorld.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our PointWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> baseline is a deterministic,
recurrent PTv3 dynamics model, obtained by adapting PointWorld to operate on
complete 3D point clouds and to be applied recurrently
(Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Baselines ‣ Appendix B Model, Training, and Baseline Details ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>). It is trained on the same data, for a
number of action-conditioned training windows matched to GPWM’s,
conditions on the actuator’s motion, and predicts the motion of the rest of
the scene; longer horizons are rolled out by chaining 16-frame
predictions, each starting from the previous prediction.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Planners</h3>

<section id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-entropy method.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Noise CEM and both Action CEM variants use the same cross-entropy method
(<span id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CEM</span>) and differ only in what it searches over. Each round draws
<math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> candidates from a Gaussian, rolls all of them out over the full
horizon, and refits the Gaussian to the best eighth of the candidates.
We use the elite-retention and variance-floor modifications of
iCEM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pinneri et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. The best-scoring candidate found over all
rounds is the plan that is executed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Noise CEM.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The CEM variable is the noise of GPWM’s sampler. We use a stochastic
sampler, which draws fresh noise at every denoising step, so the searched
noise is the initial draw together with these per-step draws. With a
deterministic (ODE) sampler only the initial noise would remain, and
noise-space planning applies to either. Every candidate is a complete
generated trajectory, and the plan is its actuator motion.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F19" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><img src="2611.08338v1/Guidance_Step.png" id="A5.F19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:215/77;" width="215" height="77" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F19.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 19</span>: </span><span id="A5.F19.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Guidance step with streaming lookahead.<span id="A5.F19.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
For a gradient step on noisy sample <math id="A5.F19.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we get an estimate of the clean trajectory using streaming lookahead. Backpropagating through the lookahead allows guidance to optimize for long horizon tasks with sparse rewards only on the final frame.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent noise optimization.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LNO optimizes the same noise by gradient ascent on the reward, with the
weights of GPWM frozen (Fig. <a href="#A5.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ Noise CEM. ‣ E.3 Planners ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>). The streaming
sampler strides the model window across the full horizon of <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> frames,
and the terminal reward
<math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=-\lVert c(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{T})-g\rVert_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=-\lVert c(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{T})-g\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> on the predicted object
centroid is backpropagated through every model call. LNO first draws a
pool of at least 32 random samples and keeps the best <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>; each is then refined
with <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I=5</annotation></semantics></math> AdamW steps (learning rate 0.1, gradient clipping at 1.0, and
a small penalty that keeps the noise statistically Gaussian). The member
with the highest predicted reward is executed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Action CEM.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both world models are searched in the same action space: the actuator’s
per-frame motion along the degrees of freedom it uses in the training
data. This is the rod’s planar translation for Pushing, the paddle’s
translation and yaw for Pile Manipulation, and the hand’s 6-DoF motion
plus gripper opening for Picking (the two fingers share one command).
Candidates are sampled independently per frame, and to keep motions in
distribution every step is clipped to the 99th percentile of the recorded
steps, both during planning and at execution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling the planning budget.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A planner can spend more time in several ways: more candidates per CEM
round (<math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>), more CEM rounds (<math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>), more LNO members (<math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>), or more
gradient steps per LNO member (<math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>). For each planner we sweep the setting
that we found empirically to give the best performance for its planning
time, and keep the others fixed (Table <a href="#A5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Scaling the planning budget. ‣ E.3 Planners ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Noise
CEM and Action CEM with GPWM sweep <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> fixed at three
rounds, so the two search spaces are compared at identical settings. LNO
sweeps <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I=5</annotation></semantics></math>; for low planning budgets we also decrease the size of the initial screening pool. PointWorld sweeps <math id="A5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A5.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="A5.T6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Planner settings<span id="A5.T6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> swept by each curve in

<math id="A5.T6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>: CEM candidates per round; <math id="A5.T6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>: CEM rounds; <math id="A5.T6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>: LNO members refined with
5 gradient steps each. LNO’s smallest budgets decrease the screening pool and take no gradient steps.</span></span></figcaption>

</table>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.4 </span>Execution</h3>

<div id="A5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For noise-space planning, the plan is the actuator motion that GPWM
generates. At every frame we fit a rigid pose to the predicted actuator
particles (Kabsch alignment to the actuator’s initial geometry), and the
simulator tracks these poses open-loop: the rod and the paddle by pose
control, and the Franka hand as a floating base together with its gripper
opening. For action-space planning, with either world model, the planned
per-frame actions are executed directly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.5 </span>Additional Analysis of Planning Results</h3>

<section id="A5.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Predicted versus executed progress.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Predicted versus executed progress. ‣ E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> compares each planner’s progress as
predicted by its world model with the progress it achieves in
simulation. Noise-space plans lose part of their predicted progress on
Pushing and Picking but keep most of it, and on Pile Manipulation their
predictions carry over almost exactly. Action-space plans predict
progress on every task and achieve almost none, with the exception of
PointWorld on Pile Manipulation. Figure <a href="#A5.F21" title="Figure 21 ‣ Pushing and Picking. ‣ E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a> shows each
planner’s predicted and simulated outcomes on Pile Manipulation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A5.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="A5.T7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Predicted and executed task progress<span id="A5.T7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> (%), at each
task’s planning budget: progress in the world model’s own rollout of the
chosen plan <math id="A5.T7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> progress after open-loop execution in
simulation.</span></span></figcaption>
<table id="A5.T7.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A5.T7.6.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T7.6.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="A5.T7.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Planner</span></td>
<td id="A5.T7.6.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A5.T7.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pushing</span></td>
