</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pushing and Picking.</h4>

<div id="A5.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Action-space search in either world model does not find the contact
sequence these tasks require, and Table <a href="#A5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Predicted versus executed progress. ‣ E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows
that it fails differently on the two tasks. On Pushing, the search fails
to find progress even inside the world models: its chosen plans are
predicted to make only 23–37% progress, against 89–94% for
noise-space plans. Under a sparse terminal reward, random per-frame
motions that bump the block without pushing it toward the target give the
search little to improve on, and the rod rarely moves around the block.
On Picking, the search does find plans the world models rate highly
(78–98% predicted progress), but none of that progress occurs in
simulation. No progress is possible before a grasp, and a grasp is hard
to discover in the high-dimensional space of hand and gripper motions.
The search instead settles on plans whose predicted object motion comes
from exploiting errors in the predicted dynamics.
Noise-space plans in GPWM move the rod behind the block before
pushing and grasp before lifting; these contact sequences come from the
learned interaction prior, not from raw search over actions
(Figs. <a href="#A5.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ Pushing and Picking. ‣ E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a> and <a href="#A5.F22" title="Figure 22 ‣ Pushing and Picking. ‣ E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>).
PointWorld’s predictions for its chosen Picking plans show the object
rising to the target while the gripper stays 3–12 cm away from it
(Fig. <a href="#A5.F23" title="Figure 23 ‣ Pushing and Picking. ‣ E.5 Additional Analysis of Planning Results ‣ Appendix E Planning ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F20" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/appendix_planning_push_failures.png" id="A5.F20.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/234;" width="476" height="234" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F20.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 20</span>: </span><span id="A5.F20.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Pushing.<span id="A5.F20.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Executed plans at the 100 s budget on two
scenarios. LNO in GPWM moves the rod around the block and pushes it onto
the target. Action CEM, with GPWM or PointWorld, produces jittering rod
motions that leave the block where it is.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A5.F21" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/appendix_planning_pile_failures.png" id="A5.F21.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/298;" width="476" height="298" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F21.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 21</span>: </span><span id="A5.F21.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Pile Manipulation.<span id="A5.F21.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Each planner’s predicted outcome and the
outcome of executing the same plan in Genesis, at the 200 s budget. LNO’s
predicted push carries over to the simulator almost unchanged.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A5.F22" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/appendix_planning_pick_failures.png" id="A5.F22.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/240;" width="476" height="240" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F22.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 22</span>: </span><span id="A5.F22.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Picking.<span id="A5.F22.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Executed plans at the 200 s budget for two

Franka arm is rendered for visualization only; plans are executed with a
floating hand.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A5.F23" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/appendix_planning_pick_pointworld_prediction.png" id="A5.F23.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/186;" width="476" height="186" alt="Refer to caption">

</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Predictions from a Single Image</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section gives the details of the predictions from single images in
Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Generalization across Geometry and Physics ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> and more examples.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Reconstruction and Setup</h3>

<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reconstruction.</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SAM 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carion et al., 2025</a>)</cite> segments each object named in a text prompt,
SAM 3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">SAM 3D Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite> reconstructs it as a mesh, and MoGe-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>
estimates the metric depth and camera that place the meshes in the scene.
Each object is represented by 1,024 particles sampled on its surface, as in
the training data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scale, materials, and release.</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each scene is rescaled so that its objects match the particle spacing of the training
objects, by 1.7 times for the desk photograph, and times are reported at the
original scale. Each object is assigned a material type and a Young’s
modulus. The four
given frames describe free fall from the chosen release pose.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Rendering.</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Image pixels of moving objects are filled with
LaMa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suvorov et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Each object mesh follows its predicted
particles, every vertex moving with its four nearest particles, and is path
traced with the camera of the image. Sand is drawn as grains, and sand
particles that end below the table are drawn on its surface.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>More Examples</h3>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A6.F24" title="Figure 24 ‣ F.2 More Examples ‣ Appendix F Predictions from a Single Image ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">24</span></a> shows more drops from the desk photograph and
from five generated images, two of them stylized images beyond the training
data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F24" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/more_drops_from_images.png" id="A6.F24.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:410/500;" width="410" height="500" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F24.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 24</span>: </span><span id="A6.F24.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">More drops from images.<span id="A6.F24.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Each row shows the input image with
the simulated objects outlined, their particles at the last input frame, and
three predicted frames. Row 1, the lemon from the desk photograph falls onto
the toy car as an elastic, a plasticine, and a sand object, shown 1.53 s after
release. Row 2, a plasticine ball lands on the pepper, rolls off and pushes it
aside. Rows 3 to 7 use generated images. Row 3, an elastic gummy bear falls
onto a plasticine donut on a dorm desk, flattens and slides off. It stays
flattened, a limitation of the model for soft elastic objects. Row 4, an
elastic gel cube falls onto a pile of Mars regolith simulated as sand and
scatters it. Row 5, an elastic jelly cube falls onto sprinkles simulated as
sand, and the gummy bear beside it slumps by 1.53 s, the same limitation. Row 6, in a claymation scene, a plasticine
tomato lands on an elastic one, and the two topple and come to rest apart.
Row 7, in a 1970s photograph, an elastic lemon lands on an elastic jelly mold
and comes to rest on top. Rows 6 and 7 are stylized images beyond the
training data. Young’s moduli are 10 kPa for the gummy bears, donut, gel
cube, bread roll, jelly cube, and jelly mold, 1 MPa for the toy car and the
block, and 100 kPa for all other objects. The car, pepper, block, and tennis
ball are elastic. Times are at each scene’s original scale.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Changing the Observed History</h3>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model receives four frames of history, so editing them changes the
predicted future. In Figure <a href="#A6.F25" title="Figure 25 ‣ F.3 Changing the Observed History ‣ Appendix F Predictions from a Single Image ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">25</span></a> a ball dropped onto a pepper comes
to rest on top. We then rewrite only the ball’s four input frames so that it
moves sideways at 9 cm/s from where it rests, and let the model continue. No
actuator is modeled.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F25" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/nudge_directions.png" id="A6.F25.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/379;" width="476" height="379" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F25.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 25</span>: </span><span id="A6.F25.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Changing the observed history.<span id="A6.F25.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Every row continues the same
drop of the blue ball onto the pepper. In the top row the ball is released,
lands, and rests on top at 0.35 s, when we freeze the scene. Without an edit
it stays there. In each row below, only the ball’s four input frames at the
freeze are rewritten so that it moves in the direction of the green arrow (the
edited ball is drawn orange), and the model predicts the rest. Times are since
the release at the original scale. The last column is 1.44 s after the
freeze.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Dragging a Reconstructed Object</h3>

<div id="A6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#A6.F26" title="Figure 26 ‣ F.4 Dragging a Reconstructed Object ‣ Appendix F Predictions from a Single Image ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a>, a sloth reconstructed from a photograph is
dragged into a foam star. Every model receives the same initial scene and
commanded drag, and the arrow shows the drag direction.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F26" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/sloth_star.png" id="A6.F26.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/142;" width="476" height="142" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F26.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 26</span>: </span><span id="A6.F26.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Dragging a sloth into a foam star.<span id="A6.F26.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> A sloth reconstructed from a photograph is dragged into a foam star, and every model gets the same start and drag. The arrow shows the commanded drag. Objects are drawn with dense points that follow each model’s predicted particles.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.5 </span>Folding Garments from Generated Images</h3>

<div id="A6.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A6.F27" title="Figure 27 ‣ F.5 Folding Garments from Generated Images ‣ Appendix F Predictions from a Single Image ‣ GPWM : Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">27</span></a> applies the Garment Folding specialist to
garments from generated images. Each garment is segmented from a top-down
image, represented as two cloth layers at the particle spacing of the training
data, and placed on the most similar training garment, which sets its size and
supplies the recorded gripper motion. The specialist predicts all frames
from that motion, which moves the grasped edge 16 to 20 cm, so each garment
ends in a partial fold.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F27" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.08338v1/fold_from_image.png" id="A6.F27.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/172;" width="476" height="172" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F27.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 27</span>: </span><span id="A6.F27.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Folding garments from generated images.<span id="A6.F27.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The grippers
(orange) follow the motion recorded for a training garment, and their points
are given to the model.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section><div class="ltx_rdf" about="" property="dcterms:creator" content="Robert Ren, Matthew Bronars, He Zhu, Yikai Tang, Jianing Zhang, Sergey Zakharov, Pavel Tokmakov, Katerina Fragkiadaki"></div>
<div class="ltx_rdf" about="" property="dcterms:title" content="GPWM: Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion"></div>

</article>
</div>
